newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan herbal medicine firm seeks London listing.
newsitem.headline: Japan herbal medicine firm seeks London listing.

text.p: After more than 120 years in business, a Japanese maker of oriental medicines is planning its first ever market listing -- in London.

By listing on the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM), Kenshodo Pharmaceuticals Ltd aims to tap into the vast market in Europe for herbal medicine, which the industry estimates is potentially three times larger than that in Japan itself.

Kenshodo would become the first Japanese firm to list shares overseas without first doing so at home. It will also be the first Japanese firm to list on AIM, a market established in 1995 for small firms and start-up ventures, which has less stringent listing criteria than some other markets.
"The environment in Japan is not very sympathetic towards small companies, unlike in other countries," Kenshodo president Tokinori Maruya told Reuters in a recent interview.

"Small- to medium-sized firms like us cannot borrow enough from banks to cover capital investment costs, yet on the other hand, Japan's direct financing rules are so tedious that many venture capitals peter out before they can get ample funds."

Maruya, who worked as an accountant in the United States for about 20 years before entering the herbal medicine business, said Kenshodo plans to boost its capital by 1.5 billion yen ($13.5 million) through the flotation, to a total of three billion yen ($27.0 million).
"We want to list our shares not only to raise funds, but also to make ourselves known in the United Kingdom and make it easier to start business there," he said.
Kenshodo was attracted to London by the speedy listing procedures on AIM and its big ambitions to expand abroad.
According to industry data, the European market for Chinese herbal medicine is potentially about three times as large as Japan's, which alone is estimated to be worth $2.1 billion.
Kenshodo plans to secure its share of this market by starting herbal medicine exports to Britain and other European countries within the year.

Maruya said the shares would likely debut on AIM in September, once preparations started in April are complete, but it will still have a long wait ahead before going public in Japan -- probably until the year to March 1999.
"Japan imposes a very long, two-to-three-year auditing period on firms before their shares can be offered for trade.
"We've decided to procure funds and start our overseas expansion by listing on an overseas market while waiting for our shares to be registered for OTC trade here."
To people accustomed to swallowing little white pills to get rid of headaches and other ailments, Chinese herbal medicine with its strange-smelling powders and tinctures may seem a little quaint.
But Kenshodo, which started its business in 1875 in western Japan, hopes that offering its shares to the public will help change that image.

"There is growing interest in herbal medicine, but most people still do not know for instance that some of it is used as ingredients for Western medicine," he said. "They still associate it with herbal medicine vendors who used to scour the hillsides of Japan for medicinal plants years and years ago."
Maruya said Kenshodo is now looking looking into a possible takeover of a firm in a similar line of business, "preferably one that is listed on the London bourse to hasten our expansion".
Should this go ahead as planned, a listing on New York's NASDAQ would be a goal in the future, he said.

In Japan itself, Kenshodo has aggressive plans to increase the number of its shops from the current 11 to 130 by 2000 and in July it will start selling natural cosmetics through a franchise deal with Britain's Nectar Overseas Ltd.
"We plan to give our herbal medicine drug stores added value by providing customers with natural beauty goods as well," Maruya said.
Kenshodo posted a parent current profit of 281 million yen ($2.53 million) in the year to March 1997 on sales of 3.1 billion yen ($27.9 million).
